title: DNS, DHCP, HTTP, email and software-defined networking
subtitle: The protocols you actually see: what happens between typing a name and seeing a page, and how modern networks are managed.

sections.title: DHCP: getting an address
sections.body: A new host has no IP. DHCP lends one in four messages, known as DORA: Discover (broadcast), Offer, Request, Acknowledge. The lease also carries the subnet mask, default gateway and DNS server, and expires unless renewed.

choices.text: The host has no address and does not know the server’s address.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Everyone on the link hears it; the server answers.

figures.caption: Figure 6.1.1 — DORA
figures.script:
diagram("mode: sequence
[New host] as h
[DHCP server] as d
h -> d : DISCOVER (broadcast)
d --> h : OFFER (192.168.1.50)
h -> d : REQUEST (I’ll take it)
d --> h : ACK (lease 8 h, gateway, DNS)");

sections.title: DNS: names to addresses
sections.body: DNS is a distributed hierarchy: root servers know the top-level domains (.com, .np), TLD servers know the domains, and the domain’s authoritative server knows the host. Your machine asks a recursive resolver, which does the walking and caches the answer for its TTL.

worked.why: A record has TTL 300 s. The resolver answered at t = 0.
A query at t = 120 s is answered from the cache; one at t = 400 s triggers a new lookup.

questions.prompt: What does a DNS TTL control?

choices.text: How long a cached answer may be reused.
How many hops the query may take.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: After it expires the resolver must ask again.

figures.caption: Figure 6.2.1 — a recursive DNS lookup
figures.note: A cold lookup walks the hierarchy; later ones hit the cache.
figures.script:
diagram("mode: sequence
[Browser] as b
[Resolver] as r
[Root] as root
[.com server] as tld
[Authoritative] as a
b -> r : www.example.com?
r -> root : who knows .com?
root --> r : ask the .com server
r -> tld : who knows example.com?
tld --> r : ask ns.example.com
r -> a : www.example.com?
a --> r : 93.184.216.34
r --> b : 93.184.216.34");

sections.title: HTTP and the web
sections.body: Typing a URL sets off a chain: DNS finds the IP, TCP connects (TLS for HTTPS), the browser sends GET /page HTTP/1.1 and the server replies with a status line, headers and the body. Methods: GET (read), POST (send), PUT, DELETE. Status families: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error (404), 5xx server error (500). HTTP is stateless; cookies and tokens carry a session.

choices.text: Each request is independent: the server keeps no memory of earlier ones by itself.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Cookies or tokens are added to recognise a user.

figures.caption: Figure 6.3.1 — a page load
figures.note: The whole trip for one page.
figures.script:
diagram("mode: sequence
[Browser] as b
[DNS] as d
[Web server] as s
b -> d : example.com?
d --> b : 93.184.216.34
b -> s : TCP handshake (+ TLS)
b -> s : GET /index.html
s --> b : 200 OK + HTML
b -> s : GET /style.css
s --> b : 200 OK + CSS");

sections.title: Email: SMTP, POP3, IMAP
sections.body: SMTP pushes mail from your client to your server and between servers. To read it, POP3 downloads messages (usually deleting them from the server) while IMAP keeps them on the server and syncs folders across devices. Other services: FTP moves files; SNMP manages devices; VoIP carries voice over IP.

questions.prompt: Which protocol keeps mail on the server so several devices stay in sync?

sections.title: Software-defined networking
sections.body: In a traditional router the control plane (route calculation) and data plane (forwarding) live together in each box. SDN separates them: a central controller computes behaviour and programs simple forwarding devices through an API (OpenFlow). Benefits: a global view, automation, rapid change. Related ideas: network virtualisation, content delivery networks (CDNs cache content near users), named-data and intent-based networking.

choices.text: The control plane from the data plane.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Logic moves to a controller; devices only forward.

figures.caption: Figure 7.1.1 — the SDN architecture

sections.title: Network security in brief
sections.body: Goals: confidentiality, integrity, authentication, availability. Tools: TLS encrypts a connection; firewalls filter by address, port or application; VPNs tunnel private traffic over the Internet; intrusion detection watches for attacks. The next-generation areas (quantum networks, network virtualisation) build on the same layered ideas.

choices.text: An encrypted, authenticated channel over TCP.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It protects against eavesdropping and tampering.

problems.prompt: List the order of events when you open https://example.com for the first time.
problems.answer: DHCP already gave your address; DNS resolves the name; TCP three-way handshake; TLS handshake agrees keys; HTTP GET; server responds 200 OK with the page; the browser fetches the page’s other resources.
